blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we have two stars for you: a robot barista that never sleeps, and an owl that can turn its head almost all the way around.
Ready?
Let's go!
In Beijing, there is a special coffee shop.
There is no human barista inside — a robot makes all the coffee, all day and all night.
You tap your order on a screen.
With a minimum wait of about twenty-five seconds, your cup is ready.
No need to yell across a noisy room — the robot reads your order and gets to work.
Let me clarify one thing: it is not a big brewery with huge tanks.
It is a small, neat machine that makes one cup at a time.
It follows the same standard steps every time: grinding the beans, pouring hot water, adding milk, and handing you the cup.
Cup by cup, the numbers accumulate: on its opening day, the little shop served 202 cups in one hour — more than three cups every minute!
Visitors often remark on how fast it is, and a group of morning customers appreciate it most at night, when every other shop is closed.
In total, the robot can work all night without feeling tired.
So, would you trust a robot to make your hot chocolate?
Now let's fly into the quiet night.
When the dark curtain of night falls, the owl wakes up.
And here is a surprise: an owl can turn its head about 270 degrees — almost all the way around — without moving its body!
Why?
First, count the bones: we have seven small bones in our necks, but an owl has fourteen — twice as many!
More bones mean more room to turn.
Second, an owl cannot move its eyes: its big eyes are fixed in their sockets, like cameras that cannot look left or right.
So the head must do all the turning, and the owl can look behind itself while its body stays still.
But wait — what causes the owl's brain to keep working when its neck twists so far?
In our necks, such a twist would squeeze the blood vessels.
The owl has a clever design: its neck bones have little air pockets, and its blood vessels have extra room and backup paths, so blood keeps flowing to the brain.
It is like a road with side streets: if one is blocked, the blood takes another.
So on a dark night, the owl turns its head, listens, and hears a tiny mouse moving in the grass.
Dinner is served — and the mouse never saw the owl move.
Today's idiom is 'spill the beans.' When you spill the beans, you tell a secret by mistake!
Here's an example: 'Lily wanted the birthday party to be a surprise, but she spilled the beans and told her brother!' Remember: if you want to keep a secret, don't spill the beans!
Let's think: a robot that makes coffee all night, and an owl that turns its head 270 degrees.
First: if a minister came to your town, what drink would you ask the robot to make for him?
Second: the owl has fourteen neck bones and we have only seven — what other animal superpower would you like to have?
Third: if you were as small as an ant, would you rather ride on the robot's arm or sit on the owl's back?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Keep reading, keep wondering, and never spill the beans!
See you tomorrow!
